items.prose: A broker's sign-up form asks for a base currency, a risk level and a statement frequency. These have 5, 3 and 2 choices. Only the GBP branch is drawn out.
items.question: How many different ways can the form be filled in?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each question is a stage, so multiply the choices.

byKey.added: You added 5, 3 and 2. Every currency goes with every risk level and every frequency, so multiply.
byKey.one-branch: You counted the GBP branch only. Each currency has 6 endings.

explain.text: The GBP branch has $3 \times 2 = 6$ endings, and so does each of the other currencies. So there are $5 \times 6 = 30$ ways.

items.prose: Seven analysts each give one talk at a research meeting, one after another.
items.question: In how many orders can the seven talks run?

options.why: You worked out $7 \times 7$. Once an analyst has spoken, only the others can take the next slot.
You added 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1. The places are stages, so they multiply.
That is $6!$, the count for six talks. The seventh analyst multiplies it by 7.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the choices for each place in the sending order.

explain.text: The first slot has 7 choices, the next 6, and so on down to 1. So there are $7! = 5040$ orders.

items.prose: A trading competition has 9 entrants. Prizes of £500, £300 and £100 go to first, second and third.
items.question: In how many ways can the three prizes be awarded?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Fill first, second and third place in turn.

byKey.repeats: You worked out $9^3$, which lets one entrant win twice.
byKey.groups: You counted the groups of three winners. The prizes differ, so who gets £500 matters.
byKey.added: You added 9, 8 and 7. The places multiply.
byKey.all: That is $9!$, which ranks all nine. Only three places win.

explain.text: First place has 9 choices, second 8 and third 7. So $P(9, 3) = \dfrac{9!}{6!} = 504$.

items.prose: A head of research picks 4 of her 9 analysts to form a working group. All members have the same role.
items.question: How many different groups could she form?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count ordered picks, then divide by the orders of each group.

byKey.ordered: You counted ordered picks. Each group of 4 appears $4! = 24$ times among them.
byKey.by-four: You divided by 4. Four people have $4! = 24$ orders.
byKey.repeats: You let one analyst be picked more than once.

explain.text: Ordered picks: $9 \times 8 \times 7 \times 6 = 3024$. Each group appears $4! = 24$ times. So there are $\dfrac{3024}{24} = 126$ groups.

items.prose: A desk hedges a position with exactly one instrument. It can use one of 4 futures or one of 6 options.
items.question: How many hedges can the desk choose from?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Is this one pick or two picks in a row?

byKey.times: You multiplied, as if the desk used a future and an option. It uses one or the other, so the lists add.
byKey.kinds: You counted the two kinds of instrument. Each kind still offers several choices.

explain.text: The hedge is a single pick from two separate lists, so the counts add: $4 + 6 = 10$. A future **and** an option would be $4 \times 6 = 24$ pairs.

items.prose: A fund beats its benchmark or not in each of the 6 months of a half-year.
items.question: How many patterns have exactly 2 winning months?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Choose which 2 of the 6 months are winners.

byKey.ordered: You picked the winning months in order. A pattern only depends on which months win.
byKey.all: You counted every pattern of the half-year, $2^6$. Only some have exactly two winning months.
byKey.count: You counted the winning months. Count the ways to choose which months they are.

explain.text: Choose the 2 winning months: $\binom{6}{2} = \dfrac{6 \times 5}{2!} = 15$. That equals $\binom{6}{4}$, because choosing the 2 winning months fixes the 4 losing ones.

items.prose: Six orders are sent one at a time. Two of them are hedges for the same position and must be sent back to back.

state.caption: HH is the two hedges taped together

items.question: How many sending orders are allowed?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tape the two hedges into one block, then count.

byKey.one-way: You lined up the 5 units but kept the hedges in one order. Either hedge can go first, which doubles it.
byKey.ignored: That is every sending order, including those that split the hedges.
byKey.small: You used $4!$ for the units. The block and the other 4 orders make 5 units.

explain.text: The hedge block and the 4 other orders are 5 units: $5! = 120$ orders. Inside the block either hedge can go first. So there are $120 \times 2 = 240$.

items.prose: Some counts depend on order and some do not.
items.question: Which of these counts change when you swap two of the chosen items? Select all that apply.

options.text: A 4-digit PIN with no repeated digit
A chair and a deputy from 6 traders

options.why: Each stock gets the same weight, so swapping two gives the same portfolio.

options.text: A committee of 4 members with equal votes
options.why: The seats are the same, so swapping two members gives the same committee.

feedback.correct: Rankings, PINs and named roles depend on order.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether swapping two chosen items gives a different result.

explain.text: Swapping first and second place, two PIN digits, or chair and deputy changes the result: those are permutations. Swapping two stocks of equal weight, or two equal members, changes nothing: those are combinations.

items.prose: A trading login code is 3 different letters from A to Z, then 1 digit from 0 to 9.
items.question: How many login codes are there?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the letters as ordered picks, then multiply by the digit stage.

byKey.repeats: You let the letters repeat. The three letters must be different.
byKey.no-digit: You counted the letters but left out the digit. It multiplies by 10.
byKey.groups: You counted sets of letters. ABC and CBA give different codes.

explain.text: The letters are an ordered pick: $P(26, 3) = 15\,600$. The digit is a new stage with 10 choices. So there are $15\,600 \times 10 = 156\,000$ codes.
